batch_name: Edward Kelley, Bosome Book, and the Ripleian Circle in Bohemia
description: Edward Kelley (d. 1597), John Dee's associate and alchemical practitioner at Rudolf II's court; the Bosome Book (the personal commonplace book of George Ripley discovered by Samuel Norton in 1574); and two events documenting the departure of Dee and Kelley for the Holy Roman Empire (1583) and the Kelley circle's promotion of Ripleian alchemy in Bohemia (1583-1597). Primary source: Jennifer M. Rampling, 'John Dee and the Alchemists: Practising and Promoting English Alchemy in the Holy Roman Empire,' Studies in History and Philosophy of Science 43:3 (2012) pp.498-508.

persons.name: Edward Kelley
persons.bio_html:
Edward Kelley (1555–1 November 1597), also spelled Kelly, was an English alchemist and occultist who became John Dee's partner in angelic communication and alchemical practice, and who subsequently established a career as a professional alchemist at the court of Emperor Rudolf II in Prague. His date and place of birth remain uncertain; he is sometimes identified with an 'Edward Talbot' mentioned in Dee's diaries before 1582, a detail that has generated speculation about a possible earlier identity. Jennifer M. Rampling, in 'John Dee and the Alchemists' (Studies in History and Philosophy of Science 43:3, 2012), provides the most detailed scholarly account of Kelley's alchemical activities in Bohemia and his role in promoting English Ripleian alchemy on the continent.

Kelley arrived at Dee's household at Mortlake in 1582, initially in the role of a scryer or medium capable of receiving communications from angelic beings in Dee's scrying sessions. Within two years he had become Dee's regular collaborator in both angelic consultations and laboratory alchemy. Kelley accompanied Dee, his family, and Albrecht Łaski (palatine of Sieradz) when they departed England on 21 September 1583. The English party settled first briefly in Cracow, then in Prague, and eventually in Třeboň (Wittingau) as clients of Vilém of Rožmberk (1535–1592), one of the greatest magnates in Bohemia and, like Emperor Rudolf II, a major patron of alchemists.

By 1587, Kelley's independent reputation as an alchemical adept had begun to eclipse Dee's. He claimed to have performed convincing transmutations of base metals into gold, some in the presence of Rudolf II himself, and his claimed noble Irish ancestry was validated by a knighthood from the Emperor. Kelley's rise is mirrored by a rapid increase in the circulation and prestige of the works of George Ripley (d. ca. 1490) in East Central Europe. Rampling argues that Kelley consciously deployed Ripleian authority as intellectual capital in his relationships with patrons and colleagues: by compiling, copying, and presenting Ripley's works as gifts to powerful contacts, he positioned himself as heir to a venerable English alchemical tradition. In 1589, for instance, Kelley compiled a Latin manuscript of seven Ripleian works for presentation to the Silesian imperial councillor Karl von Biberstein (1528–1593), inscribing it with the dedication: 'Edward Kelley wrote this book out of kindness and love for his most sincere friend, the noble lord Karl von Biberstein... whom he wishes to have known as his adopted philosophical son.' The German alchemist Nicolaus Mai composed a verse translation of Ripley's Compound of Alchymy (Compound of Alchymy) at Kelley's instigation for presentation to Rudolf II.

Dee departed Bohemia in early 1589, but Kelley remained, pursuing his alchemical career and corresponding with alchemical patrons across the Empire, including Moritz, Landgraf of Hesse-Kassel. He was eventually imprisoned by Rudolf II in circumstances that remain poorly documented, and died on 1 November 1597 — reportedly following a failed attempt to escape from custody. Kelley's posthumous influence on European alchemy was substantial: the manuscripts he assembled, annotated, and distributed circulated through the Bohemian alchemical networks after his death, and when Ludwig Combach compiled the Opera Omnia Chemica of George Ripley (Kassel, 1649) sixty years later, he attributed several works to Kelley as translator. Elias Ashmole, gathering material for the Theatrum Chemicum Britannicum (London, 1652), preserved Kelley's legacy alongside Ripley's in the English alchemical canon.

texts.title: Bosome Book (George Ripley)
texts.analysis_html:
The Bosome Book (also styled Besome Book, Vade mecum, Ripley's Secret Bosom Book, or Liber secretus Georgii Riplaei) is a Latin commonplace book of alchemical notes, recipes, and jottings attributed to George Ripley (d. ca. 1490) and described in the manuscript tradition as Ripley's personal working notebook — the private record of his alchemical practice. Jennifer M. Rampling, in the 'Catalogue of the Ripley Corpus' (Ambix 57:2, 2010, CRC 3), notes that this text is the core manuscript collection of Ripleian materials and that its discovery marked a key moment in the formation of the English alchemical canon. The same Rampling, in 'John Dee and the Alchemists' (Studies in History and Philosophy of Science 43:3, 2012, pp.498-508), provides evidence for the Bosome Book's role in the continental reception of Ripley's alchemy.

The Bosome Book was discovered on 20 July 1577 by the English alchemist Samuel Norton (1548–1621), grandson of Thomas Norton (author of the Ordinal of Alchemy), who announced the find in his alchemical treatise, the Key of Alchemie, dedicated to Elizabeth I. Norton described the manuscript as 'the secret bosome booke of Riple, whereby the true grounds are discovered' and set about translating it into English as of February 1574 (old style). Although the original Latin manuscript is no longer extant — only a single later copy survives in British Library MS Harley 2411 — Norton's English translations circulated widely in the second half of the sixteenth century. John Dee owned and transcribed excerpts from these English versions, including two texts entitled 'George Ryppley's bosome booke or Vademecum' and the 'Practise by experiment', preserved in Bodleian Library MS Ashmole 1486 (Part V).

The contents of the Bosome Book are composite and include a substantial body of practical sericonian recipes (procedures based on the dissolution of 'sericon' or minium in vinegar), together with theoretical aphorisms attributed to Ripley's main authority Guido de Montanor (the 'Notable rules from Guido') and several subsidiary practical tracts: the Elixir vitae (on the production of the drinkable, medicinal gold or aurum potabile), the Concordantia Guidonis et Raimondi (Concordantia Guidonis et Raimondi), and the Accurtations of Raymond. These materials were reworked into the Viaticum seu varia practica Georgii Riplaei — a collection of practical extracts that appeared in continental Europe in the early seventeenth century and was printed by Ludwig Combach in the Opera Omnia Chemica (Kassel, 1649). The appearance of these Bosome Book extracts in Prague by ca. 1600 — in the manuscripts of Nicolaus Mai and Simon Budek — is connected by Rampling to the activities of Edward Kelley, who took a proportion of Dee's alchemical library to Bohemia in 1583 and actively distributed copies of Ripleian works among his alchemical patrons and colleagues.

events.title: Dee and Kelley depart England for the Holy Roman Empire
events.description: 21 September 1583, Mortlake/London: John Dee and Edward Kelley depart England for the Holy Roman Empire, accompanied by Dee's family and the Polish nobleman Albrecht Łaski (palatine of Sieradz), whose pretensions to the Polish throne had received encouragement in the angelic conversations mediated by Kelley at Mortlake. The English party takes with them a substantial proportion of Dee's vast library — approximately 800 books — including alchemical manuscripts and works attributed to George Ripley. Jennifer M. Rampling, in 'John Dee and the Alchemists' (Studies in History and Philosophy of Science 43:3, 2012), identifies the departure as a turning point in the European reception of English Ripleian alchemy: the books Dee carried to the continent would pass through Kelley's hands into the collections of alchemical practitioners in Bohemia, seeding the networks that produced the first printed editions of Ripley's Latin works sixty years later. The party makes an inauspicious start at Cracow and Prague before settling in Třeboň (Wittingau) as clients of Vilém of Rožmberk (1535–1592), one of the greatest alchemical patrons in Bohemia.

events.title: Kelley's Ripleian alchemical circle in Bohemia
events.description: ca. 1583–1597, Třeboň and Prague: Edward Kelley, settled first in Třeboň and later at the court of Emperor Rudolf II in Prague, establishes himself as a leading alchemical practitioner in the Holy Roman Empire, performing transmutations — some in the Emperor's presence — and building a network of alchemical clients and patrons in which the works of George Ripley (d. ca. 1490) play a central role. Jennifer M. Rampling, in 'John Dee and the Alchemists' (Studies in History and Philosophy of Science 43:3, 2012), documents Kelley's systematic promotion of Ripleian authority as social and intellectual capital: he compiled manuscript anthologies of Ripleian works as gifts for powerful patrons, including a collection of seven Ripleian texts (Ksiaznica Cieszynska SZ DD.vii.33) inscribed with a dedication to the Silesian councillor Karl von Biberstein (1528–1593) on 2 August 1589; he encouraged the German alchemist Nicolaus Mai to produce a verse translation of Ripley's Compound of Alchymy for presentation to the Emperor; and he served as the conduit through which the Bosome Book and the Viaticum (practical extracts from the Bosome Book) entered Bohemian alchemical circulation. The consequence of Kelley's activities was a significant Bohemian reception of English alchemical texts: nine Ripleian works were transcribed in Bohemia in 1605–06 by the alchemist Simon Thadeas Budek, and the manuscript tradition Kelley had fostered provided primary exemplars for Ludwig Combach's printed edition of Ripley's Opera Omnia Chemica (Kassel, 1649).
